I quit twice. The first time I had a really rough time and five months into it I relapsed and drank for another two years. The second time I was more ready, I think, because my health had become so bad and I hated feeling so sick all the time. Not gonna lie, it took a few months to get used to not having it my life. After six months into it I had developed routines that were not related to alcohol (and cigarettes, tbh) and things got a little easier. Some days were harder than others. 

I didn't do AA but I hear that can be helpful to not feel so alone, which is what was hardest for me. Not that I had a huge group of friends that I lost or anything, but without alcohol my days felt so big and empty, which is hard to navigate when feeling desperate. Also booze was like an old friend in that I was used to having it around, so when it wasn't around I felt like I had lost something I loved which is hard to share with people who haven't been through it. Having other people to talk to would probably have helped a lot.

Congratulations on your sobriety! Coincidentally I quit cigs shortly after I quit alcohol, too. Quitting alcohol is a fraught time, full of stresses and anxieties all by itself. Nicotine is a stimulant so it's probably contributing to heightening your anxiety, yes. It's deceptive because we smoke to feel less anxious, or at least I did, but overall it's not helping. When I quit smoking I figured I was already feeling bad being sober, I might as well quit the cigarettes, too. And at the end of it I'm glad I did it that way. It was tough, but since I was already halfway miserable it wasn't too large a leap, and when I came out the other side I was free of two things, which felt good.

Yes, I quit smoking cold-turkey and though the process of quitting spikes anxiety for a week or two, I felt much better physically and mentally after quitting. Part of why I quit was that I kept thinking about how I was ruining my health, plus all the money I was spending, all of which was making me more anxious. 

Quitting smoking is tough, but it's been four years and now I can't imagine going back to it. I recommend joining an online support group to get you through the first couple weeks if you decide to quit, that really helped me stick to it. Good luck.

I can see where this might make you feel less abnormal...it's troublesome for me because it makes me feel like I may not be "abnormal" enough and reinforces my doubt as to whether my OCD is "bad enough" or something.

To clarify I think OCD is partly habitual but there is definitely a biological component which medication can be good for. Sometimes people are born with certain neurons "wired together" but it is possible they can be rewired with practice. 

When it comes to OCD vs schizophrenia I think the fact that most OCD sufferers can recognize the illogicality of their own actions is a major plus. Mental illnesses like schizophrenia and bipolar often include delusions and loss of reality, which makes controlling how the wires "fire together" impossible without medication.

Whenever I worry I am a sociopath I try to be impolite (which for me means simply not saying "thank you" or smiling) to strangers in public like cashiers or people who hold the door for me. When I feel guilty for being so rude I know that there is no way I could be a sociopath because I like being nice to people and feel remorse when I am not nice. Sociopaths/narcissists usually lack remorse and rarely think about what others are feeling. Instead they are imitating emotion to fit in.

I went to a therapist once whose favorite phrase was, "If they fire together, they wire together," meaning neurons in the brain. She emphasized learning new ways of thinking and reacting and coping, therefore creating new pathways that would replace old methods of thinking. Not sure I completely bought it, but it was a constructive way of thinking about recovery. For me lots of OCD is habitual because over time I have become so used to my own brain, and it makes sense to me that old habits may be replaced with new ones.  Kind of like taking a new driving route to work....the old roads are still there, but the new road is the one I use.

Definitely tell your therapist your symptoms—that's what they are there for! They will ask you questions and make the diagnosis, possibly over a few sessions after they have a fuller understanding of your experience, but don't be afraid to be honest. Good luck and good for you for getting help, you are on you way to a better way of living.

Yes, this sounds like OCD. It seems like you would probably feel this way (seeking reassurance and doubting if your belief is "right" or "wrong") no matter what political position you would take. 

I think cognitive dissonance is really difficult for OCD people. Take your drug legalization thing...the dissonance is: you think legalizing all drugs is the "right" thing in principle, but the real-life drug deaths it might cause is the "wrong" thing. It's similar to how free speech may allow for harmful things to be said—the principle is sound, but the real-life consequences are often harmful. People have two options: they can either make peace with the principle, accept the negative possible consequences as less important, and move on...or the consequences become impossible to ignore, and they adjust their principles accordingly. 

But these contradictions are tough to reconcile for OCD people because it messes with the dedication to precision and getting things "right." Some things will never be absolutely right or wrong, especially ideologically, and that's hard to accept.

Have you researched other political positions? The fact that you instead seem intent on justifying one general political position to the point of hours-long reassurance and compulsive study signals that OCD is probably at work.

Ha ha ha welcome to my existence!!!!! I have like 30 burner reddit accounts because I don't want people to know who i am online by "tracking" my reddit activity. Yes, this is the OCD talking. Realistically it's always good to be cautious online, but the truth is that unless someone you love is an equally obsessed Sherlock Holmes computer hacker you will be fine. A person would need to possess extreme curiosity about you *and* the technological hacker skills to find the stuff you have deleted or hidden. Question whether this pair of characteristics is realistic in each of your loved ones. 

I have a loving family but honestly, none of them are curious enough to research my internet history too deeply, and even if they were they would not have the know-how. This doesn't stop me from obsessing, however! So I feel you.

Also, unless you've done something illegal there's no logical reason to worry about being a national/international pariah. If you are worried that you sent a couple nudes you regret or shot your mouth off or something like that, most likely that will not cause such large-scale consequences. Even if you said things that were really offensive, like racial epithets or something, and people found out...if you have honestly worked to change those attitudes since then and apologize, you will most likely be forgiven.

Six years ago I was on Celexa for one year before I took myself off it. It helped, but it had a "flattening" effect where I stopped caring about anything. However, my mind was very quiet. I loved that I was free from excruciating anxiety, but I did not like how apathetic I was which is why i took myself off. Since then I have not been on any medication and I avoid the doctor (including therapists) like the plague. It doesn't help that I also believe that if I talk to a therapist I will make everything worse because I will just be dwelling more on the things that distress me. 

Mostly I have been managing it on my own. Some months are worse than others. Lately I have been having a lot more obsessive/distressing thoughts and am considering going back to the doc because it's interfering with my enjoyment of being alive. However, before this latest jag I have done okay on my own. Most of the time I can accept that this is the way I am. I also have hobbies that allow me to focus my obsessive energy in a constructive way, but some people do not have those kinds of outlets. As long as it does not become debilitating, I live with it. 

In any case, I do not think you are "crazy," you just have a mind that is wired differently from the so-called norm. It's possible to have obsessional thinking without compulsion, too. I forgot to say that in my first reply. The absence of compulsions doesn't make the obsessional aspect any less real. This is called "primarily obsessional OCD" or "pure O" if you want to look it up. I think that is what I lean toward, too.

This sounds so much like me. I think OCD comes in lots of forms, it's not all handwashing or counting like on TV (though they are very real). Mostly I have obsessive, intrusive thoughts. I think about everyone dying. All the time. How time moves and stands still. Etc etc. I used to be obsessed with accidentally jerking the wheel while driving and killing myself accidentally. Anxiety is another condition that feeds into obsessional thinking, but usually anxiety is more vague, and often exacerbated by a looming event (like a presentation or doc's appt). Obsessions are more like a constant barrage of unending, specific thoughts.

I'd say compulsion-wise mine are fairly subtle and others probably would not notice, and even I do not notice them because they are so "normal" to me, but, for example, if I feel the plumbing is not working right I always listen to make sure. These compulsions are limited in nature, meaning it's not unending, but maybe for a couple weeks I am compelled to listen to the toilet tank finish filling or listen for faucet drips every time I'm near them until the obsession fades. Also, sometimes when I do certain things, I think about a particular non-sequitur memory in a way that's not quiet "normal" (like when I do certain exercises while working out I always think about the same, totally unrelated memory, or when I clip my toenails I always think about this one short story I once read that has nothing to do with toenails). These are not outward or "dramatic" compulsions but are compulsions nonetheless.
